newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-British Steel profit seen hit by stg.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-British Steel profit seen hit by stg.

text.p: British Steel Plc's annual pre-tax profits are expected to be knocked sharply lower by a strong pound on Monday, June 16, amid speculation the group may announce thousands of job cuts to reduce costs.
Analysts said Britain's biggest steel maker must accelerate the speed of its cost-cutting programme to maintain profitability.

Profit forecasts for the group have been consistently downgraded in the last few months to compensate for the devastating effect of the strong pound, which is trading around a five-year high against the Deutsche mark and other major European currencies.

In March this year, a spokesman for British Steel admitted sterling's appreciation had a significant impact on the company's profits. "Eighty percent of our sales are affected by the strong pound", he had said.
Pre-tax profits for the year ending March 31, 1997, are expected to be between 380 and 575 million stg with a consensus forecast of 460 million stg, according to Reuters Securities 3000 data.
Most analysts predicted an unchanged dividend of 10p.
The steelmaker, with an output of about 16 million tonnes a year, posted a pre-tax profit of 1.1 billion stg on sales of 7.85 billion stg the previous year.
The steady rise of the sterling has sent the shares tumbling around 20 percent over the past 10 months amid a series of broker downgrades.
Technical analysts said the stock, which was trading at 160-3/4, up 4-3/4p by 1045 GMT on Friday, remained in a downward trend.
"The strong pound has cost them a lot of revenue and profit", Terence Sinclair, steel analyst at Salomon Brothers said.
And as about 55 percent of the groups sales are generated outside the UK, British Steel has no other choice than to go ahead with cost-cutting.

"That (the strong pound) does not go away", Sinclair said, urging British Steel "to accelerate" its restructuring. He saw little help from steel prices in Europe, which are expected to rise by about ten percent in the third quarter of the current year.
In reaction to the surge of sterling, British Steel in March announced it would cut "significantly more than 5000 jobs in the next five years" at costs of tens of million pounds.

Chairman Brian Moffat had warned steel unions of the need for job cuts and more flexible working practices. Talks between British Steel, which employs about 53,000 people worldwide, including 43,000 in the UK, and the unions are continuing.
Tim Bennet, steel analyst at Morgan Stanley, believed the charges for cost-cutting programmes in the past and the current financial year would be 40 million stg per annum.

Demand in steel would be strong but Bennet expected only "modest price increases" adding the company would remain "exposed" as sterling's strength continued to hit exports and lure foreign competitors into the UK.
Analysts' forecasts for pre-tax profit for the current financial year ending March, 1998 range between 95 and 400 million stg.
